claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: WT and Stat6 KO BMDMs can similarly activate Akt and mTORC1 in response to IL-4.
claims.source: Conversely, WT and Stat6 KO BMDMs could similarly activate Akt, as indicated by phosphorylation on S473, as well as mTORC1, as indicated by phosphorylation of the mTORC1 target S6K, in response to IL-4 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The Jak-Stat and Akt-mTORC1 pathways are independent signaling branches downstream of the IL-4R.
claims.source: These findings support the idea that the Jak-Stat and Akt-mTORC1 pathways are independent signaling branches downstream of the IL-4R, and suggest a basis by which all M2 genes are controlled by Stat6 while a subset receives additional inputs from the Akt-mTORC1 pathway.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing independent activation of Stat6 and Akt-mTORC1 pathways.

claims.claim: IL-4 treatment enhances global acetylation of H3 and H4 histones in BMDMs.
claims.source: Indeed, IL-4-treatment of BMDMs enhanced global acetylation of H3 and H4 histones, as indicated by western blot of whole cell lysates (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: IL-4-inducible increases in global H3 and H4 acetylation are reduced by Akt inhibitor cotreatment.
claims.source: Importantly, IL-4-inducible increases in global H3 and H4 acetylation were reduced by cotreatment with an Akt inhibitor, indicating at least partial dependence on Akt (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: Tubulin acetylation is not modulated by IL-4 treatment.
claims.source: In contrast, tubulin acetylation was not modulated by IL-4 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: IL-4 treatment increases H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of M2 genes.
claims.source: IL-4 treatment increased H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of M2 genes (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), with the degree of inducible acetylation correlating fairly well with the degree of gene induction (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2D, 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Akt inhibitor reduces H3 and H4 acetylation at Akt-dependent M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not at Akt-independent M2 genes (Chi3l3, Cd36, Fabp4).
claims.source: Interestingly, such increases in H3 and H4 acetylation were reduced by an Akt inhibitor at M2 genes induced in an Akt-dependent manner (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2), but not at M2 genes induced independently of Akt (Chi3l3, Cd36, Fabp4) (Figure 2D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: Pol II recruitment to M2 gene promoters parallels H3 and H4 acetylation and is controlled by Akt at Akt-dependent M2 genes.
claims.source: Pol II recruitment to M2 gene promoters paralleled H3 and H4 acetylation, and was controlled by Akt at M2 genes induced in an Akt-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: IL-4 treatment leads to a maximal increase in Ac-CoA levels of approximately 40-75%.
claims.source: Using quantitative stable isotope dilution-LC-MS, we found that IL-4 treatment led to a maximal increase in Ac-CoA levels of ~40–75% (Figure 3A,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS data in Figure 3A and 3C.

claims.claim: IL-4 treatment stimulates the activating phosphorylation of Acly in an Akt-dependent manner.
claims.source: Akt has been shown to phosphorylate and activate Acly (Berwick et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2014), and we found that in M2 macrophages, IL-4 treatment stimulated the activating phosphorylation of Acly in an Akt-dependent manner (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Berwick et al., 2002 and Lee et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Cotreatment with Akt or Acly inhibitors blocks IL-4-mediated increases in Ac-CoA levels.
claims.source: Importantly, cotreatment with Akt or Acly inhibitors blocked the IL-4-mediated increases in Ac-CoA levels (Figure 3C), indicating Akt- and Acly-mediated control of Ac-CoA production in M2 macrophages.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Citrate accumulates in the presence of Akt or Acly inhibitors.
claims.source: Conversely, citrate, the substrate for the Acly reaction, accumulated in the presence of the inhibitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: IL-4 treatment enhances 13C (M+2) Ac-CoA labeling from glucose, palmitate, and glutamine tracers.
claims.source: IL-4 treatment enhanced 13C (M+2) Ac-CoA labeling regardless of the tracer, indicating that all three metabolic fuels contributed to the elevated Ac-CoA pool.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by carbon tracing LC-MS data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Palmitate is the major carbon source for Ac-CoA in M2 macrophages.
claims.source: The highest labeling was observed in BMDMs fed palmitate. While LC-MS does not specifically measure the nuclear-cytosolic pool of Ac-CoA, these data suggests that palmitate may be the major carbon source for histone acetylation in M2 macrophages (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from carbon tracing data in Figure 3D showing highest labeling with palmitate.

claims.claim: The Acly inhibitor SB-204990 reduces IL-4-mediated induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Chi3l3, Fabp4, Cd36).
claims.source: Indeed, the Acly inhibitor SB-204990 reduced IL-4-mediated induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Chi3l3, Fabp4, Cd36) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: SB-204990 treatment attenuates IL-4-mediated increases in H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of Akt-dependent M2 genes but not Akt-independent M2 genes.
claims.source: Moreover, SB-204990 treatment attenuated IL-4-mediated increases in H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of Akt-dependent M2 genes, but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: SB-204990 treatment diminishes Pol II recruitment at Akt-dependent M2 genes.
claims.source: Likewise, SB-204990 treatment diminished Pol II recruitment at Akt-dependent M2 genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The p300 inhibitor C646 reduces induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, the p300 inhibitor C646 reduced induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: p300 may link the Akt/Acly-dependent rise in Ac-CoA levels to increased histone acetylation and gene induction at some Akt-dependent M2 genes.
claims.source: Therefore, p300 may link the Akt/Acly-dependent rise in Ac-CoA levels to increased histone acetylation and gene induction at some Akt-dependent M2 genes, while distinct HATs at Akt-independent genes are insensitive to such modulation of Ac-CoA levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the p300 inhibitor data and knowledge about p300's sensitivity to Ac-CoA levels.

claims.claim: Arginase activity is regulated by Acly and Akt.
claims.source: Consistent with effects on induction of Arg1, arginase activity was regulated by Acly and Akt (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by arginase activity assay data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Akt and Acly inhibitors reduce induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes in peritoneal-elicited macrophages.
claims.source: Additionally, Akt and Acly inhibitors reduced induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes in peritoneal-elicited macrophages, indicating that control of M2 activation by the Akt-Acly axis may be applicable to multiple macrophage populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes is deficient in BMDMs lacking Raptor.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes was deficient in BMDMs lacking Raptor, a defining subunit of the mTORC1 complex (Dibble and Manning, 2013). In contrast, induction of Akt-independent M2 genes was not reduced (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 5A and a citation to Dibble and Manning, 2013.

claims.claim: Raptor-deficient BMDMs express lower levels of Acly protein.
claims.source: mTORC1 is known to stimulate Acly expression (Porstmann et al., 2008; Düvel et al., 2010), and we found that Raptor-deficient BMDMs expressed lower levels of Acly protein (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5B and citations to Porstmann et al., 2008 and Düvel et al., 2010.

claims.claim: BMDMs with constitutive mTORC1 activity from Tsc1 deletion display elevated Acly levels that are reduced by rapamycin treatment.
claims.source: Conversely, BMDMs with constitutive mTORC1 activity resulting from deletion of Tsc1 (Byles et al., 2013), a negative regulator of mTORC1 (Dibble and Manning, 2013), displayed elevated Acly levels that were reduced by treatment with the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citations to Byles et al., 2013 and Dibble and Manning, 2013.

claims.claim: IL-4-inducible Acly phosphorylation is reduced in Raptor-deficient BMDMs.
claims.source: Additionally, we noted that IL-4-inducible Acly phosphorylation was reduced in Raptor-deficient BMDMs (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The Akt-mTORC1 axis controls Acly activating phosphorylation and protein levels.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that the Akt-mTORC1 axis controls Acly activating phosphorylation and protein levels, likely contributing to its control of M2 activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on Akt and mTORC1 regulation of Acly.

claims.claim: mTORC1 activity is greatly reduced in amino acid deficient media and intermediate in media containing low levels of amino acids.
claims.source: As expected, mTORC1 activity, as assessed by phosphorylation of its downstream target S6K, was greatly reduced in amino acid deficient media and intermediate in media containing low levels of amino acids (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Increasing amino acid levels augments Akt activation.
claims.source: In line with (Tato et al., 2011; Novellasdemunt et al., 2013), increasing amino acid levels also augmented Akt activation, as indicated by enhanced phosphorylation on two critical residues, T308 and S473 (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B and citations to Tato et al., 2011 and Novellasdemunt et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Titrating amino acids has no effect on Stat6 phosphorylation and activation.
claims.source: Titrating amino acids had no effect on Stat6 phosphorylation and activation (Figure 6B), validating the use of this experimental model to modulate the Akt-mTORC1 axis independent of canonical Stat6 signaling.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Amino acid levels dose dependently increase Acly phosphorylation and protein levels.
claims.source: Consistent with effects on mTORC1 and Akt activity, amino acid levels dose dependently increased Acly phosphorylation and protein levels (Figure 6B) as well as Ac-CoA production (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B and LC-MS data in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Amino acids potentiate induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes.
claims.source: Importantly, amino acids potentiated induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The effect of amino acids on M2 gene induction is at least partially Raptor-dependent.
claims.source: This effect of amino acids was at least partially Raptor-dependent, indicating a critical role for mTORC1 in this process (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Culture in leucine-deficient media attenuates IL-4-inducible mTORC1 and Akt activity and Acly phosphorylation, but not Stat6 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Culture in leucine-deficient media attenuated IL-4-inducible mTORC1 and Akt activity and Acly phosphorylation, but not Stat6 phosphorylation (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Leucine deficiency selectively reduces expression of Akt-dependent M2 genes.
claims.source: Importantly, leucine deficiency selectively reduced expression of Akt-dependent M2 genes (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Akt activation is increased in the fed state compared to the fasted state in the ATM-containing stromal vascular fraction of white adipose tissue.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that Akt activation was increased in the fed state compared to the fasted state in the ATM-containing stromal vascular (SVF) fraction of the white adipose tissue (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Global H3 acetylation and M2 gene expression are elevated in the fed state in adipose tissue macrophages.
claims.source: Although we were unable to reliably detect pAcly or Acly in the SVF for technical reasons, global H3 acetylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B) and M2 gene expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) followed a similar pattern and were elevated in the fed state.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B and qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: IL-13 expression is increased in the fed state.
claims.source: Expression of all M2 genes was elevated in the fed state (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), consistent with an important role for IL-13, a critical regulator of ATM M2 polarization (Odegaard and Chawla, 2011) that is increased in the fed state (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D), in feeding-induced ATM polarization, although postprandial elevations in nutrients like amino acids and glucose may also contribute.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D and a citation to Odegaard and Chawla, 2011.

claims.claim: 758 genes were induced >2.0 fold by IL-4 in BMDMs.
claims.source: In the RNA seq analysis, 758 genes were induced >2.0 fold by IL-4, of which 91were downregulated >30% by both Akt and Acly inhibitors (including Arg1, Retnla, and Mgl2), confirming critical roles for Akt and Acly in control of M2 activation as well as substantial overlap in the activities of the two proteins (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: 91 IL-4-inducible genes were downregulated >30% by both Akt and Acly inhibitors.
claims.source: In the RNA seq analysis, 758 genes were induced >2.0 fold by IL-4, of which 91were downregulated >30% by both Akt and Acly inhibitors (including Arg1, Retnla, and Mgl2), confirming critical roles for Akt and Acly in control of M2 activation as well as substantial overlap in the activities of the two proteins (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: Most genes sensitive to Acly inhibitor are sensitive to Akt inhibitor (91/118).
claims.source: In contrast, most genes sensitive to Acly inhibitor were sensitive to Akt inhibitor (91/118). This indicates that in the context of M2 activation, Acly is a major target of Akt and is critically controlled by Akt activity, likely in regulation of Ac-CoA production and histone acetylation at M2 genes (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: Cell cycle and DNA replication pathways are preferentially enriched among the 91 Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes.
claims.source: Gene enrichment analysis of the 91 Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes identified preferential enrichment of several pathways, including cell cycle and DNA replication (Figure 7C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data in Figure 7C and 7D.

claims.claim: Chemokines are enriched in Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes, including Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl17, and Ccl24.
claims.source: Interestingly, chemokines were also enriched in Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes (Figure 7C–D), including Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl17, and Ccl24.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data in Figure 7C and 7D.

claims.claim: Akt- and Acly-dependent induction of CCL17 and CCL24 was confirmed by qRT-PCR and ELISA.
claims.source: Akt- and Acly-dependent induction of CCL17 and CCL24 was confirmed by qRT-PCR and ELISA (Figure 7E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 7E and ELISA data in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Ear2, Ear11, and Ear12 genes are coregulated by the Akt-Acly pathway.
claims.source: Finally, genes in the eosinophil associated ribonucleases (Ear) family were found to be regulated by Akt and Acly. While barely missing the stringent cutoffs that we set for the RNA-seq analysis, qPCR analysis confirmed coregulation of Ear2, Ear11, and Ear12 genes by the Akt-Acly pathway (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: IL-4 signaling co-opts the Akt-mTORC1 pathway to regulate Acly, leading to increased histone acetylation and M2 gene induction.
claims.source: Here we show that IL-4 signaling co-opts the Akt-mTORC1 pathway to regulate Acly, a key enzyme in Ac-CoA synthesis, leading to increased histone acetylation and M2 gene induction.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Only a subset of M2 genes is controlled by the Akt-mTORC1-Acly pathway, including those regulating cellular proliferation and chemokine production.
claims.source: Only a subset of M2 genes is controlled in this way, including those regulating cellular proliferation and chemokine production.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the RNA-seq and gene enrichment analysis data.

claims.claim: Metabolic signals impinge on the Akt-mTORC1 axis for control of M2 activation.
claims.source: Moreover, metabolic signals impinge on the Akt-mTORC1 axis for such control of M2 activation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the amino acid titration and leucine deficiency experiments.

claims.claim: Akt-mTORC1 signaling calibrates metabolic state to energetically demanding aspects of M2 activation.
claims.source: We propose that Akt-mTORC1 signaling calibrates metabolic state to energetically demanding aspects of M2 activation, which may define a new role for metabolism in supporting macrophage activation.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined experimental findings.

claims.claim: M1 macrophages upregulate glucose and glutamine utilization.
claims.source: For example, M1 macrophages upregulate glucose and glutamine utilization (Tannahill et al., 2013; Cramer et al., 2003), while M2 macrophages augment β-oxidation and glutamine consumption (Vats et al., 2006; Jha et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tannahill et al., 2013 and Cramer et al., 2003.

claims.claim: M2 macrophages augment β-oxidation and glutamine consumption.
claims.source: For example, M1 macrophages upregulate glucose and glutamine utilization (Tannahill et al., 2013; Cramer et al., 2003), while M2 macrophages augment β-oxidation and glutamine consumption (Vats et al., 2006; Jha et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vats et al., 2006 and Jha et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Increased glycolytic flux in M1 macrophages is coupled to de novo lipogenesis, which enables ER and Golgi expansion and production of high levels of inflammatory cytokines.
claims.source: Increased glycolytic flux in M1 macrophages is coupled to de novo lipogenesis, which enables ER and Golgi expansion and production of high levels of inflammatory cytokines (Everts et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Everts et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Enhanced glycolysis in M1 macrophages leads to accumulation of succinate, resulting in stabilization of HIF-1α and transcriptional induction of Il1b.
claims.source: Another consequence of enhanced glycolysis is accumulation of the TCA cycle metabolite succinate, leading to stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α and transcriptional induction of Il1b and other target genes in the M1 macrophage (Tannahill et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tannahill et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Glutamine metabolism fuels production of UDP-GlcNAC, an important modification of multiple M2 markers.
claims.source: How oxidative metabolism boosts M2 activation is not clear, but glutamine metabolism fuels production of UDP-GlcNAC, an important modification of multiple M2 markers (Jha et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jha et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Akt mediates enhanced glycolysis to support lipid synthesis and inflammatory cytokine secretion in M1 macrophages.
claims.source: For example, Akt mediates enhanced glycolysis to support lipid synthesis and inflammatory cytokine secretion in M1 macrophages (Everts et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Everts et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Akt stimulates glucose-fueled lipid synthesis in growing and proliferating cells, where lipids are used to build cellular membranes.
claims.source: Akt similarly stimulates glucose-fueled lipid synthesis in growing and proliferating cells, where lipids are used to build cellular membranes (Robey and Hay, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Robey and Hay, 2009.

claims.claim: In cancer cells and differentiating adipocytes, metabolic state is linked to gene expression via effects on histone acetylation.
claims.source: A seminal study from Wellen and colleagues indicated that in cancer cells and differentiating adipocytes, metabolic state is linked to gene expression via effects on histone acetylation (Wellen et al., 2009), thus we hypothesized that Akt may control histone acetylation to regulate M2 gene expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wellen et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Acly cleaves cytosolic citrate to produce a nuclear-cytoplasmic pool of Ac-CoA.
claims.source: A key regulator of Ac-CoA production is the enzyme Acly, which cleaves cytosolic citrate to produce a nuclear-cytoplasmic pool of Ac-CoA (Wellen et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wellen et al., 2009 and established biochemical knowledge.

claims.claim: The activity of some HATs, including p300, is regulated by Ac-CoA levels and metabolic status.
claims.source: The activity of some HATs, including p300, is regulated by Ac-CoA levels and metabolic status (Mariño et al., 2014; Pietrocola et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mariño et al., 2014 and Pietrocola et al., 2015.

claims.claim: mTORC1 activity in macrophages is controlled by amino acid levels, ADP/ATP levels, and other metabolic inputs.
claims.source: The Akt-mTORC1 pathway is a major metabolic sensor, and mTORC1 activity in particular is controlled by amino acid levels, ADP/ATP levels, and other metabolic inputs (Dibble and Manning, 2013; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dibble and Manning, 2013 and Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claims.claim: Amino acids directly and potently regulate mTORC1 activity independent of the TSC complex.
claims.source: Amino acids directly and potently regulate mTORC1 activity independent of the TSC complex (Dibble and Manning, 2013; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012) and can also activate Akt in some contexts (Tato et al., 2011; Novellasdemunt et al., 2013), hence we varied amino acid concentrations as a way to modulate Akt-mTORC1 activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dibble and Manning, 2013 and Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claims.claim: Leucine is particularly critical in regulation of mTORC1 activity.
claims.source: We also examined M2 activation using the complementary model of leucine deprivation, since leucine is particularly critical in regulation of mTORC1 activity (Hara et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hara et al., 1998.

claims.claim: ATM M2 polarization is thought to critically maintain insulin sensitivity in white adipose tissue.
claims.source: ATM M2 polarization is thought to critically maintain insulin sensitivity in white adipose tissue, so such feeding-induced increases in M2 activation may coordinate responses to nutrient influx to mediate metabolic homeostasis in the postprandial state (Odegaard and Chawla, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Odegaard and Chawla, 2011.

claims.claim: p300 has a high Km for Ac-CoA and is responsive to changes in Ac-CoA levels.
claims.source: Its high Km (Mariño et al., 2014; Pietrocola et al., 2015) may allow p300 to link metabolic status and Akt/mTORC1 activity, in the form of Ac-CoA levels, to histone acetylation and transcriptional induction at some M2 genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mariño et al., 2014 and Pietrocola et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Aberrantly increased mTORC1 activity in Tsc1-deficient BMDMs attenuates M2 activation.
claims.source: In seeming contrast to these data indicating that mTORC1 supports M2 activation, we and others have shown that aberrantly increased mTORC1 activity in Tsc1-deficient BMDMs attenuates M2 activation (Byles et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Byles et al., 2013 and Zhu et al., 2014.

claims.claim: In obesity, chronic nutrient excess leads to an aberrant increase in mTORC1 activity that contributes directly to insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation.
claims.source: Downstream of the insulin receptor, such context-dependent roles of mTORC1 are well-established. In lean/healthy animals, mTORC1 critically mediates insulin signaling in metabolic tissues (to coordinate postprandial nutrient storage), but in obesity, chronic nutrient excess leads to an aberrant increase in mTORC1 activity that contributes directly to insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claims.claim: Ac-CoA can be synthesized independently of the Akt-mTORC1-Acly axis by AceCS1 or nuclear pyruvate dehydrogenase.
claims.source: Alternatively, Ac-CoA can be synthesized independently of the Akt-mTORC1-Acly axis by AceCS1 (Hallows et al., 2006) or nuclear pyruvate dehydrogenase (Sutendra et al., 2014) to mediate histone acetylation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hallows et al., 2006 and Sutendra et al., 2014.

claims.claim: AceCS1 activity is controlled by SIRT1, providing a means for Ac-CoA production and histone acetylation in conditions of low energy or nutrients.
claims.source: AceCS1 activity is controlled by SIRT1, thus providing a means for Ac-CoA production and histone acetylation in conditions of low energy or nutrients (Hallows et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hallows et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Ear2 and Ear11 are thought to have chemoattractant activity for dendritic cells and macrophages.
claims.source: Ear genes are of interest because Ear2 and Ear11 are thought to have chemoattractant activity for dendritic cells and macrophages and are known to be highly induced in settings of Type 2 inflammation (Cormier et al., 2002; Yamada et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cormier et al., 2002 and Yamada et al., 2015.

claims.claim: M2 macrophages play a key role in metabolic homeostasis, parasite infection, allergic diseases, and wound healing and tissue repair.
claims.source: As M2 macrophages play a key role in metabolic homeostasis, parasite infection, allergic diseases, and wound healing and tissue repair (Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013; Odegaard and Chawla, 2011), these findings are relevant for metabolic control of macrophage function in diverse contexts.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013 and Odegaard and Chawla, 2011.

claims.claim: The Akt-mTORC1 pathway has a well-established role in promoting anabolic metabolism in growing/proliferating cells, tumor cells, and metabolic tissues.
claims.source: The Akt-mTORC1 pathway has a well-established role in promoting anabolic metabolism in growing/proliferating cells, tumor cells, and metabolic tissues.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claims.claim: In the context of cellular proliferation, Akt-mTORC1 activity couples growth factor signaling and nutrient availability to the synthesis of proteins, lipids, and nucleotides.
claims.source: In the context of cellular proliferation, for example, Akt-mTORC1 activity couples growth factor signaling and nutrient availability to the synthesis of proteins, lipids, and nucleotides (Dibble and Manning, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dibble and Manning, 2013.

claims.claim: A critical role for Akt-mTORC1 signaling in activated CD8 T cells is to support their migration to sites of inflammation.
claims.source: Interestingly, previous studies have shown that a critical role for Akt-mTORC1 signaling in activated CD8 T cells is to support their migration to sites of inflammation (Finlay and Cantrell, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Finlay and Cantrell, 2011.

results.result: Metabolomics profiling of M2 macrophages reveals enrichment in pathways including urea cycle, arginine and proline metabolism, glycolysis, amino sugar metabolism, and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are directly supported by LC/MS-based metabolomics data presented in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1. The enrichment analysis is appropriately conducted and the findings are consistent with prior literature on M2 macrophage metabolism (C1 cites Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013).

results.result: IL-4 treatment increases glucose uptake and metabolism in M2 macrophages in an Akt-dependent manner, with both glycolysis and oxidative metabolism enhanced. Glycolysis inhibition reduces M2 gene induction, while Akt does not control β-oxidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 are well-supported by multiple experimental approaches including 3H-deoxy-D-glucose uptake assays (Figure 1B), extracellular flux analyses (Figure 1C), qPCR with metabolic inhibitors (Figure 1D), and β-oxidation assays (Figure 1E). The use of pharmacological Akt inhibitor MK2206 provides consistent evidence for Akt-dependent control of glucose metabolism but not β-oxidation.

results.result: Akt activity selectively controls induction of a subset of M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not others (Chi3l3, Cd36, Fabp4). The Jak-Stat6 and Akt-mTORC1 pathways function as independent signaling branches downstream of IL-4R.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C13 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 2A), western blots showing independent activation of Stat6 and Akt pathways (Figure 2B), and luciferase reporter assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C). The use of Stat6 KO BMDMs and Akt inhibitors demonstrates pathway independence. The selective gene regulation pattern is reproducible with structurally distinct Akt inhibitors.

results.result: IL-4 treatment enhances global and gene-specific histone H3 and H4 acetylation in an Akt-dependent manner at Akt-dependent M2 genes but not Akt-independent M2 genes. Pol II recruitment parallels histone acetylation patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 are supported by western blot data showing global histone acetylation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) and ChIP data demonstrating gene-specific acetylation patterns (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D). The specificity control showing no effect on tubulin acetylation (C16) strengthens the conclusion. The correlation between histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment is well-documented.

results.result: IL-4 treatment increases Ac-CoA levels by approximately 40-75% through Akt-dependent phosphorylation and activation of Acly. Akt or Acly inhibitors block IL-4-mediated Ac-CoA increases and cause citrate accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are supported by quantitative LC-MS measurements of Ac-CoA (Figure 3A,C), western blots showing Akt-dependent Acly phosphorylation (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and metabolomics data showing citrate accumulation with inhibitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). The use of siRNA controls validates antibody specificity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

results.result: Carbon tracing experiments show that glucose, palmitate, and glutamine all contribute to the elevated Ac-CoA pool in M2 macrophages, with palmitate showing the highest labeling and potentially being the major carbon source.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by 13C-labeled substrate tracing experiments analyzed by LC-MS (Figure 3D). However, the authors appropriately note that LC-MS does not specifically measure the nuclear-cytosolic pool, making C25 somewhat inferential. The conclusion that palmitate is the major source is reasonable but should be considered tentative.

results.result: Acly inhibition selectively reduces IL-4-mediated induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes and their associated histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment. The p300 HAT may link Ac-CoA levels to histone acetylation at Akt-dependent genes. This regulation extends to arginase activity and peritoneal macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 are supported by qPCR data with Acly inhibitor SB-204990 (Figure 4A), ChIP data (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), p300 inhibitor experiments (Figure 4C), arginase activity assays (Figure 4D), and experiments in peritoneal macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The use of structurally distinct Acly inhibitors validates specificity. C30 is appropriately presented as inferential based on known p300 properties.

results.result: mTORC1 regulates M2 activation through control of Acly protein levels and phosphorylation. Raptor-deficient BMDMs show reduced Akt-dependent M2 gene induction and lower Acly expression, while Tsc1-deficient BMDMs show elevated Acly levels that are rapamycin-sensitive.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 are supported by qPCR data from Raptor knockout BMDMs (Figure 5A), western blots showing Acly protein levels (Figure 5B), and complementary experiments with Tsc1 deletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The genetic approaches using conditional knockouts provide strong evidence. C37 is appropriately presented as an integrative conclusion from the combined data.

results.result: Amino acid levels dose-dependently modulate Akt-mTORC1-Acly axis activity and Ac-CoA production, selectively potentiating induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes in a Raptor-dependent manner, without affecting Stat6 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by western blots showing dose-dependent effects of amino acids on pathway activation (Figure 6B), LC-MS measurements of Ac-CoA (Figure 6C), qPCR data (Figure 6D), and experiments in Raptor knockout cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The experimental design appropriately validates that amino acid titration modulates Akt-mTORC1 independently of Stat6 signaling.

results.result: Leucine deficiency attenuates IL-4-inducible mTORC1, Akt, and Acly activity without affecting Stat6 phosphorylation, and selectively reduces expression of Akt-dependent M2 genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by western blot data (Figure 6E) and qPCR analysis (Figure 6F). The leucine deprivation model complements the amino acid titration experiments and is well-justified given leucine's critical role in mTORC1 regulation (cited to Hara et al., 1998).

results.result: In adipose tissue macrophages, Akt activation, global H3 acetylation, and M2 gene expression are elevated in the fed state compared to fasted state, correlating with increased IL-13 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by western blot data from stromal vascular fraction (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B) and qPCR data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D). The authors appropriately note technical limitations in detecting pAcly/Acly in SVF. The correlation with IL-13 levels provides mechanistic context, though the authors appropriately acknowledge that postprandial nutrients may also contribute.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis reveals that 758 genes are induced >2-fold by IL-4, with 91 genes downregulated >30% by both Akt and Acly inhibitors. Most Acly-sensitive genes (91/118) are also Akt-sensitive, indicating Acly is a major Akt target in M2 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 7A,B) with appropriate statistical cutoffs (>2 RPKM, Log2fold>1.0, DESeq P-adj<0.05). The overlap analysis between Akt and Acly inhibitor effects is well-presented. The conclusion that Acly is a major Akt target is appropriately inferred from the high proportion of overlap.

results.result: Gene enrichment analysis of the 91 Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes identifies cell cycle, DNA replication, and chemokine pathways. Akt-Acly regulation of CCL17, CCL24, and Ear family genes is confirmed by qPCR and ELISA.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by KEGG pathway and Gene Ontology enrichment analysis (Figure 7C,D) and validated by qPCR (Figure 7E) and ELISA (Figure 7F). The enrichment analysis is appropriately conducted using DAVID. The validation of specific genes strengthens confidence in the RNA-seq findings.

results.result: IL-4 signaling co-opts the Akt-mTORC1 pathway to regulate Acly, leading to increased histone acetylation and selective M2 gene induction. Only a subset of M2 genes (including those regulating proliferation and chemokines) is controlled this way, with metabolic signals impinging on the Akt-mTORC1 axis to calibrate M2 activation to metabolic state.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 represent integrative summary conclusions supported by the collective experimental data throughout the manuscript. C59 is appropriately presented as a proposed model. The conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches including metabolomics, genetics, pharmacology, and transcriptomics.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about macrophage metabolism, Akt-mTORC1 signaling, histone acetylation, and metabolic regulation of gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C83 are background/context claims supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the scientific foundation for the current work and are appropriately referenced.

results.result: The authors claim that IL-4 treatment increases Ac-CoA levels by 40-75% (C20), stimulates Acly phosphorylation in an Akt-dependent manner (C21), and that Akt or Acly inhibitors block IL-4-mediated increases in Ac-CoA (C22). These claims form the mechanistic core linking Akt activation to Ac-CoA production via Acly.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised a major concern about timing inconsistencies: 'AKT phosphorylation increases within 15 min of IL-4 stimulation, histone acetylation increases by about 4 hours, while pACLY increases by 6 hours, and acetyl-CoA by 8 hours.' This temporal sequence does not support the proposed model where pAcly should be directly downstream of Akt and precede histone acetylation. Reviewers requested examination of all parameters in the same time course experiment to clarify the model.

results.result: The authors claim that mTORC1 (via Raptor) controls M2 gene induction (C33), regulates Acly protein levels (C34, C35), and controls Acly phosphorylation (C36), concluding that the Akt-mTORC1 axis controls both Acly phosphorylation and protein levels (C37).
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned the physiological contribution of mTORC1, noting: 'Based on the data, it doesn't look like mTORC1 is a major contributor to the IL-4-driven pathway, since mTORC1 is implicated in regulating ACLY protein levels and ACLY protein levels do not increase with IL-4.' They asked whether the authors agree that 'the data don't appear to support mTORC1 as a major physiological component of the mechanism,' despite mTORC1 being included as a major component of the paper's conclusions.

results.result: The authors claim that IL-4 enhances global and promoter-specific H3 and H4 histone acetylation (C14, C17), that this is reduced by Akt inhibition (C15, C18), and that Pol II recruitment parallels acetylation and is Akt-controlled at Akt-dependent genes (C19).
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not explicitly critique the histone acetylation data, their concern about timing ('histone acetylation increases by about 4 hours, while pACLY increases by 6 hours, and acetyl-CoA by 8 hours') indirectly questions whether the proposed mechanism (Akt→Acly→Ac-CoA→histone acetylation) can explain the observed histone acetylation timing. The temporal inconsistency undermines confidence in the mechanistic link.

results.result: The authors claim that Akt controls a subset of M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not others (Chi3l3, Cd36, Fabp4) (C8, C9), that Akt inhibition does not affect Stat6 activation (C10, C11), that Stat6 KO does not affect Akt/mTORC1 activation (C12), and that these are independent signaling branches (C13).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these claims about the independence of Jak-Stat and Akt-mTORC1 pathways or the differential gene regulation. The summary states the study 'shows that Act stimulation in macrophages by IL-4...enhances histone acetylation and induction of a subset of the M2 genes,' implicitly accepting the subset specificity.

results.result: The authors claim that Acly inhibition reduces Akt-dependent M2 gene induction (C26), attenuates histone acetylation at these genes (C27), diminishes Pol II recruitment (C28), and that p300 inhibition similarly affects Akt-dependent genes (C29), suggesting p300 links Ac-CoA to histone acetylation (C30). Arginase activity is also regulated by Acly and Akt (C31).
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not directly critique the Acly inhibitor data, their fundamental concern about the timing of Acly phosphorylation and Ac-CoA production relative to histone acetylation casts doubt on whether Acly is the primary mechanism linking Akt to histone acetylation in the proposed timeframe. The mechanistic interpretation depends on resolving the temporal inconsistencies.

results.result: The authors claim that amino acid levels modulate mTORC1 and Akt activity (C38, C39) without affecting Stat6 (C40), increase Acly phosphorylation and Ac-CoA production (C41), potentiate Akt-dependent M2 gene induction in a Raptor-dependent manner (C42, C43), and that leucine deficiency attenuates this pathway and reduces Akt-dependent gene expression (C44, C45).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the amino acid modulation experiments. The summary acknowledges that 'this Act effect is subject to modulation by metabolic signals, which probably serves to adjust the differentiation state and function of macrophages to nutrient availability,' indicating acceptance of these findings.

results.result: The authors report RNA-seq analysis showing 758 IL-4-inducible genes (C49), with 91 downregulated by both Akt and Acly inhibitors (C50), and that most Acly-sensitive genes are Akt-sensitive (C51). Gene enrichment analysis identified cell cycle, DNA replication, and chemokine pathways (C52, C53), with validation of CCL17, CCL24, and Ear genes (C54, C55).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the RNA-seq data or the identification of co-regulated gene sets. These findings are presented as confirmatory evidence ('confirming critical roles for Akt and Acly in control of M2 activation') and were not questioned in the review.

results.result: The authors claim that in adipose tissue macrophages, Akt activation, H3 acetylation, and M2 gene expression are elevated in the fed versus fasted state (C46, C47), and that IL-13 expression is increased in the fed state (C48).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these in vivo observations. These data support the physiological relevance of the pathway but are presented as correlative evidence rather than mechanistic proof.

results.result: The authors claim that IL-4 increases glucose uptake in a time-dependent manner (C3), that Akt inhibitor reduces this uptake (C4), that enhanced glucose consumption is associated with Akt-dependent increases in glycolysis and oxidative metabolism (C5), that glycolysis inhibitor 2-DG reduces some M2 gene induction (C6), and that Akt does not control β-oxidation (C7).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these metabolic characterization data. These findings establish the metabolic context for M2 activation and the role of Akt in glucose metabolism, which are accepted as background for the main mechanistic claims.

results.result: The authors report metabolomics profiling showing enrichment of urea cycle, arginine and proline metabolism (C1), and glycolysis, amino sugar metabolism, and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism pathways (C2) in M2 macrophages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the metabolomics profiling data. These are descriptive findings that characterize the metabolic state of M2 macrophages and provide context for subsequent mechanistic studies.

results.result: The authors claim that tubulin acetylation is not modulated by IL-4 treatment, serving as a specificity control for histone acetylation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this control experiment, which demonstrates specificity of the IL-4 effect on histone acetylation.

results.result: The authors claim that citrate accumulates in the presence of Akt or Acly inhibitors, consistent with Acly's role in converting citrate to Ac-CoA.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this biochemical validation of Acly inhibition. This finding supports the mechanism by which Acly inhibitors work.

results.result: The authors claim that IL-4 enhances 13C Ac-CoA labeling from glucose, palmitate, and glutamine tracers (C24), with palmitate showing the highest labeling, suggesting it may be the major carbon source for Ac-CoA in M2 macrophages (C25).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the carbon tracing experiments. These data identify metabolic fuel sources for Ac-CoA production, though the authors acknowledge the limitation that LC-MS does not specifically measure the nuclear-cytosolic pool.

results.result: The authors claim that Akt and Acly inhibitors reduce induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes in peritoneal-elicited macrophages, suggesting the mechanism applies to multiple macrophage populations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this extension to another macrophage population. This finding supports the generalizability of the mechanism.

results.result: The authors present summary claims that IL-4 co-opts the Akt-mTORC1 pathway to regulate Acly, leading to histone acetylation and M2 gene induction (C56), that only a subset of M2 genes is controlled this way (C57), that metabolic signals impinge on this axis (C58), and propose that Akt-mTORC1 calibrates metabolic state to M2 activation (C59).
results.evaluation: These overarching conclusions are undermined by the reviewers' major concerns about timing inconsistencies and the role of mTORC1. Reviewers questioned whether 'the proposed model truly makes sense' given the temporal sequence and whether mTORC1 is 'a major physiological component of the mechanism.' The model requires clarification before these summary claims can be fully supported.

comparisons.comparison: Both address claims C20-C22 about Ac-CoA levels and Acly phosphorylation. OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED by LC-MS and western blot data. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN due to major timing inconsistencies: pAcly increases at 6 hours and Ac-CoA at 8 hours, but histone acetylation increases by 4 hours, contradicting the proposed causal sequence where Acly→Ac-CoA should precede histone acetylation.

Both address claims C33-C37 about mTORC1's role via Raptor knockout experiments. OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED by genetic knockout data. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, questioning whether mTORC1 is 'a major physiological component' since it regulates ACLY protein levels but ACLY protein doesn't increase with IL-4, suggesting mTORC1 may not be a major contributor to the IL-4-driven pathway despite being featured prominently in conclusions.

Both address histone acetylation claims C14-C15, C17-C19. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by western blots and ChIP data. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, not directly challenging the data but questioning the mechanistic interpretation due to timing issues: histone acetylation occurs at 4 hours while pAcly increases at 6 hours and Ac-CoA at 8 hours, undermining the proposed Akt→Acly→Ac-CoA→histone acetylation mechanism.

Both address claims C8-C13 about pathway independence and differential gene regulation. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by qPCR, western blots, and luciferase assays. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, accepting that Akt stimulation enhances histone acetylation and induces a subset of M2 genes without challenging the pathway independence or gene specificity findings.

Both address Acly inhibitor experiments (C26-C31). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by qPCR, ChIP, and p300 inhibitor data. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, not directly critiquing the inhibitor data but expressing doubt about whether Acly is the primary mechanism linking Akt to histone acetylation given the temporal inconsistencies in the proposed pathway.

Both address amino acid modulation claims C38-C43. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by western blots, LC-MS, and qPCR data showing dose-dependent effects. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, acknowledging that 'Akt effect is subject to modulation by metabolic signals' to adjust macrophage function to nutrient availability.

Both address RNA-seq claims C49-C51. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical analysis. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED (along with C52-C55), presenting the RNA-seq findings as confirmatory evidence for critical roles of Akt and Acly in M2 activation without challenging the data or analysis.

Both address pathway enrichment and validation claims C52-C55. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by KEGG/GO analysis and qPCR/ELISA validation. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, accepting the RNA-seq findings and validation of co-regulated gene sets without challenge.

Both address in vivo claims C46-C48 about adipose tissue macrophages. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by western blots and qPCR from stromal vascular fraction. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, accepting these correlative observations as evidence for physiological relevance without challenging the data.

Both address overarching conclusions C56-C59. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED as integrative summary conclusions from collective data. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, stating the proposed model requires clarification due to timing inconsistencies and questioning whether mTORC1 is truly 'a major physiological component of the mechanism' as claimed.

Both address metabolic characterization claims C3-C7 about glucose metabolism and β-oxidation. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by multiple assays including glucose uptake, extracellular flux, and Akt inhibitor experiments. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, accepting these metabolic findings as established background context for the main mechanistic claims.

Both address metabolomics claims C1-C2. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by LC-MS data and enrichment analysis consistent with literature. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, accepting these descriptive metabolic profiling findings that characterize M2 macrophage metabolic state without challenge.

Both address carbon tracing claims C24-C25. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by 13C-labeled substrate tracing, noting C25 is somewhat inferential since LC-MS doesn't measure nuclear-cytosolic pools specifically. Peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, accepting the identification of palmitate as a major Ac-CoA source despite acknowledged limitations.

OpenEval R10 addresses leucine deprivation claims C44-C45, finding them SUPPORTED by western blots and qPCR. Peer R6 addresses broader amino acid modulation C38-C45, rating them SUPPORTED. Both accept the amino acid experiments, with partial overlap on C44-C45 showing agreement on leucine's role in modulating the pathway.

OpenEval R5 addresses C20-C23 including citrate accumulation (C23). Peer R12 specifically addresses C23 alone, rating it SUPPORTED as biochemical validation of Acly inhibition. Both accept this finding, though peer reviewers question the broader temporal context of Acly's role (addressed in peer R1).

OpenEval R4 addresses histone acetylation claims C14-C19 including tubulin control (C16). Peer R11 specifically addresses C16 alone, rating it SUPPORTED as a specificity control. Both accept this control experiment demonstrating IL-4 specificity for histone versus tubulin acetylation.

OpenEval R7 addresses Acly inhibitor experiments C26-C32 including peritoneal macrophages (C32). Peer R14 specifically addresses C32 alone, rating it SUPPORTED as evidence for generalizability. Both accept this extension to another macrophage population without challenge.

OpenEval R15 addresses background/context claims C60-C83 from published literature, finding them SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these are foundational claims establishing scientific context rather than novel findings requiring peer scrutiny.
